D tooBroad: Extends Haddad's claim about 'at least some' images in a set of legal manuscripts to medieval scribes' margins in general, and ignores the personal remarks (complaints about cold hands) the text mentions.

stimulus: Tomas had rehearsed the speech for weeks: the thanks to his parents, the joke about the broken oven, the line explaining why he had kept the bakery's old name even though, as he had admitted to no one, he was not sure he had the right to it. Now, standing behind the counter as the first customers filed in on reopening morning, he found he could recall none of it. It did not seem to matter. Mrs. Ilunga asked whether the rye was the same recipe, and when he said it was, she bought two loaves without another word. Tomas watched her go and understood, with something nearer relief than embarrassment, whom all that rehearsing had really been meant to convince.
stem: According to the text, what is true about Tomas?
choices: He delivers his rehearsed speech to the first customers, who seem more interested in buying bread.
He realizes that his rehearsed speech was mainly meant to reassure himself that he belonged there.
He is praised by Mrs. Ilunga for preserving the recipes that first made the bakery popular.
He concludes that customers will accept him only after he explains why he kept the old name.
explanation: Answer this in two steps. First, notice the private doubt planted early: Tomas 'was not sure he had the right to' the bakery's name. Second, read the last sentence: the person 'all that rehearsing had really been meant to convince' is Tomas himself, so the speech was for his own reassurance, not for the customers. D is the most tempting wrong choice: it states the belief Tomas held while rehearsing, which the ending shows him letting go of.

pipeline.governingClue: "he was not sure he had the right to it" combined with "understood... whom all that rehearsing had really been meant to convince."
distractorRationale: A contradictedDetail: The text states that Tomas 'could recall none of it,' so he never delivers the speech.
C unstatedEvaluative: Invents praise the text never gives; Mrs. Ilunga asks one question and buys bread 'without another word.'
D other: Treats the assumption behind Tomas's rehearsing as his final conclusion; the ending shows he gives up that belief, since the customer accepts the bakery without any explanation.

stimulus: Botanist Priya Raman knows that bumblebees shake pollen loose from tomato flowers by gripping them and buzzing rapidly. She hypothesizes that the sound vibration alone, even without a bee present, causes tomato flowers to release more pollen. To test this idea, she grew two groups of tomato plants in identical greenhouses. Every day, one group heard recordings of bee buzzing played next to its flowers, while the other group was kept in silence. She then measured how much pollen each flower in the two groups released.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Raman’s hypothesis?
choices: The flowers kept in silence released more pollen than the flowers exposed to the buzzing recordings.
The plants exposed to the buzzing recordings had darker green leaves than the plants kept in silence.
The flowers exposed to the buzzing recordings released more pollen than the flowers kept in silence.
The plants exposed to the buzzing recordings produced more flowers than the plants kept in silence.
explanation: Find the cause and the effect in the hypothesis: buzzing sound (cause) leads to more pollen released (effect). The supporting finding must show the buzzing group beat the silent group on that exact measure, pollen per flower. Only C does this. D is tempting because it also favors the buzzing group, but it measures the number of flowers, not pollen release.

pipeline.governingClue: "the sound vibration alone... causes tomato flowers to release more pollen"
distractorRationale: A oppositeResult: Silent flowers releasing more pollen is the reverse of what the hypothesis predicts, so it would weaken the hypothesis.
B unrelatedMeasuredVariable: Leaf color has no connection to the hypothesis, which is about pollen release from flowers.
D nearbyHypothesis: More flowers would support a different claim, that buzzing increases flower production, not that it makes each flower release more pollen.

stimulus: Marisol Ebbe’s 1931 poem “Winter Orchard” describes a fruit orchard during the coldest months of the year. In the poem, the speaker portrays the orchard as quiet and lifeless in winter while also expressing certainty that it will flower again:
stem: Which quotation from “Winter Orchard” most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: “When April comes, these boughs will fill with white, / And blossoms will return to greet the light.”
“The branches stand bare, and not a bird will sing, / Yet buds beneath the frost will bloom again in spring.”
“No leaf remains, no footstep breaks the snow; / The hush lies deep on every empty row.”
“In August, baskets overflow with fruit, / And children climb the trees from branch to root.”
explanation: Split the claim into two parts: (1) the orchard is quiet and lifeless in winter, and (2) the speaker is sure it will flower again. Check each choice for both parts. B has bare branches and no birdsong (part 1) and trees waiting for spring (part 2). C is the most tempting, but it covers only the silent winter scene, not the return of flowers.

pipeline.governingClue: "quiet and lifeless in winter while also expressing certainty that it will flower again"
distractorRationale: A partBOnly: It shows certainty that the orchard will bloom again but never describes the orchard as quiet and lifeless in winter.
C partAOnly: It shows the silent, empty winter orchard but expresses no certainty that it will flower again.
D other: It describes the orchard in summer, full of fruit and activity, so it matches neither the lifeless winter scene nor the promise of future flowering.
notes: Minor: B conveys renewal only indirectly ('wait for spring') and never mentions flowering, while A states the flowering explicitly. A test-taker could argue for A, though A omits the quiet, lifeless winter half of the claim. Making B's second line refer more directly to blooming (e.g., 'Yet underneath the frost, sure blossoms wait for spring') would remove any doubt.
Reviewer edit: "Yet underneath the frost they wait for s…" → "Yet buds beneath the frost will bloom ag…"

stimulus: Archaeologists have often treated mended pottery as a sign of hardship. If a household drilled holes along a crack and laced the pieces back together, the reasoning went, it must have been too poor to replace the pot. At a hillside settlement occupied some 3,000 years ago, archaeologist Leah Okafor found a pattern that sits uneasily with that view. Repaired vessels there turned up most often not in the smallest dwellings but in the largest. The mended pots were also disproportionately those decorated with an incised motif found nowhere else on the site. Moreover, clay suitable for making new vessels was plentiful nearby. Okafor suggests that, at least in this community, a repair may have marked a vessel as worth preserving for what it represented rather than for what it would have cost to replace.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Mended pottery from ancient sites generally signals that a vessel held symbolic importance, not that its owners were poor.
At one ancient settlement, repaired vessels were found more frequently in large dwellings than in small dwellings.
At one ancient settlement, mending pottery may have reflected regard for certain vessels rather than a shortage of means.
Okafor's findings at one settlement have convinced most archaeologists that repairs never indicated hardship.
explanation: The text follows a pattern: an old assumption (repairs mean poverty), counterevidence from one site (large houses, distinctive decorated pots, plentiful clay), and then a conclusion. The main idea is that conclusion, kept at its stated scope: at this settlement, repairs may signal that a vessel was valued, not that its owners were poor. Choice C matches both the claim and its hedges. A is the most tempting wrong choice, but it drops 'at least in this community' and turns a local, tentative finding into a general rule.

pipeline.governingClue: "Okafor suggests that, at least in this community, a repair may have marked a vessel as worth preserving for what it represented rather than for what it would have cost to replace."
distractorRationale: A tooBroad: Extends Okafor's conclusion to ancient sites in general, ignoring the explicit limit 'at least in this community.'
B tooNarrow: Accurately restates only one piece of evidence (the dwelling-size pattern), not the conclusion that the evidence supports.
D unstatedEvaluative: The text never describes how other archaeologists responded, and 'never indicated hardship' goes far beyond Okafor's tentative claim.

stimulus: Desmond had told his sister on the phone that the new owners could do what they liked with the farmhouse. It was only a building, he'd said, and he had not lived there in twenty years. Still, when he pulled over at the end of the gravel lane, he did not get out of the car. The porch their father had built was gone, replaced by a wide deck of pale composite boards, and someone had painted the door a cheerful yellow. He found himself counting the windows, as if one might have been taken too. After several minutes he started the engine again. Only when he reached the highway did he notice that he had been gripping the wheel hard enough to make his hands ache.
stem: According to the text, what is true about Desmond?
choices: He goes inside the farmhouse and discovers that the new owners have altered nearly every room.
Although he has claimed the farmhouse no longer matters to him, he is shaken by seeing it changed.
He is disappointed mainly because the porch his father built has been replaced with a modern deck.
He believes the new owners have ruined the farmhouse by making changes that show poor taste.
explanation: First find what Desmond says: the house is 'only a building.' Then compare it with what he does. He stays in the car, anxiously counts the windows, and grips the wheel until his hands ache. Together these details show that his claimed indifference hides real distress, which is choice B. C is the most tempting wrong choice, but it fixes on the porch alone and adds 'mainly,' which the text never supports.

pipeline.governingClue: The contrast between "It was only a building, he'd said" and his behavior: staying in the car, "counting the windows, as if one might have been taken too," and "gripping the wheel hard enough to make his hands ache."
distractorRationale: A contradictedDetail: The text states that 'he did not get out of the car,' so he never goes inside.
C tooNarrow: The porch is only one of several details he registers (the door, the windows), and nothing suggests it is the main source of his reaction.
D unstatedEvaluative: Desmond never judges the owners' taste or says the house is ruined. The text shows that he is unsettled, not that he condemns the changes.

stimulus: Many moths feed on flower nectar at night, and as they feed they carry pollen from plant to plant. Ecologist Lina Marsh suspects that outdoor lighting interferes with this process. Her hypothesis is that bright porch lights reduce the number of moth visits to nearby flowers, because moths circle the lights instead of feeding. To test this idea, Marsh studied evening primrose plants growing beside twenty houses. Ten of the houses kept their porch lights on all night, and the other ten kept their porch lights off.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researcher’s hypothesis?
choices: Evening primrose plants near houses with lights on received more nighttime moth visits than did plants near houses with lights off.
More moths were seen circling the porches of houses with lights on than circling the porches of houses with lights off.
Evening primrose plants near houses with lights on received fewer nighttime moth visits than did plants near houses with lights off.
Evening primrose plants near houses with lights on had slightly taller stems than did plants near houses with lights off.
explanation: Find the cause and the effect in the hypothesis: lights on (cause) lead to fewer moth visits to flowers (effect). The supporting finding must show that effect in the lit group compared with the unlit group. Only C shows plants near lit houses getting fewer nighttime moth visits. B is the most tempting choice, but it shows only that moths gather at lights, not that flower visits go down.

pipeline.governingClue: "bright porch lights reduce the number of moth visits to nearby flowers"
distractorRationale: A oppositeResult: More moth visits near lit houses is the opposite of what the hypothesis predicts, so it would weaken the hypothesis rather than support it.
B nearbyHypothesis: This shows only that lights attract moths, a related claim; it says nothing about whether visits to the flowers actually drop, which is the outcome the hypothesis is about.
D unrelatedMeasuredVariable: Stem height is not connected to the hypothesis, which concerns moth visits to flowers, so a difference in height neither supports nor weakens it.

stimulus: The Lantern Road is a novel by Corinne Vale. In the novel, the narrator returns to her grandmother’s farmhouse after many years away. Although the house has clearly fallen into disrepair, the narrator finds that it still feels welcoming to her:
stem: Which quotation from The Lantern Road most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: “Paint curled off the shutters in long strips, and two of the porch steps had split right down the middle.”
“The roof sagged and the windows rattled in their frames, yet the old house seemed to open its arms to me.”
“I had driven for six hours, past dry fields and empty gas stations, before I finally saw the turn for the farm.”
“The moment I stepped into the kitchen, the smell of cedar wrapped around me like a blanket from my childhood.”
explanation: Split the claim into its two parts: (1) the house is falling apart and (2) it still feels welcoming. Then check each quotation against both parts. Only B covers both: the sagging roof and rattling windows show disrepair, and "seemed to open its arms to me" shows welcome, with "yet" joining the two ideas. A is the most tempting choice because its details of decay are vivid, but it shows only the disrepair.

pipeline.governingClue: "Although the house has clearly fallen into disrepair, the narrator finds that it still feels welcoming to her"
distractorRationale: A partBOnly: The peeling paint and split steps show that the house is in disrepair, but nothing in the quotation shows that the house feels welcoming.

C other: This quotation describes the drive to the farm, not the house itself, so it shows neither the disrepair nor the welcoming feeling. It is built on the passage's mention of the narrator returning rather than on either part of the claim.
D partAOnly: The comforting cedar smell shows that the house feels welcoming, but nothing in the quotation shows that the house has fallen into disrepair.
notes: Distractor rationale wrong

The error-type labels for A and D are swapped. The claim's first part is the disrepair and its second part is the welcoming feeling. Choice A shows only the disrepair, so it should be labeled partAOnly, not partBOnly. Choice D shows only the welcoming feeling, so it should be labeled partBOnly, not partAOnly. The prose explanations themselves are correct, but the labels contradict them.

stimulus: Botanist Lucía Ferrer hypothesizes that tomato plants grown beside basil suffer fewer aphid infestations because basil releases airborne chemicals that repel aphids. To test this idea, Ferrer grew tomato plants in three greenhouse sections: one with tomatoes alone, one with tomatoes beside uncovered basil plants, and one with tomatoes beside basil plants enclosed in sealed, clear plastic cases that trap airborne chemicals.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ferrer’s hypothesis?
choices: Tomato plants beside uncovered basil had more aphids than tomato plants grown alone did.
Tomato plants beside uncovered basil produced more fruit than tomato plants grown alone did.
Tomato plants beside uncovered basil had fewer aphids than tomato plants beside sealed basil did.
The uncovered basil plants themselves had very few aphids on their own leaves.
explanation: Find the comparison the study was built for: the sealed cases block only the airborne chemicals, so they isolate the proposed cause. If tomatoes near uncovered basil have fewer aphids than tomatoes near sealed basil, the airborne chemicals made the difference, which is exactly what the hypothesis predicts. D is the most tempting wrong choice, but it shows that aphids avoid basil, not that basil protects the tomatoes.

pipeline.governingClue: The sealed cases trap airborne chemicals, so the only difference between the two basil sections is whether basil’s airborne chemicals reach the tomatoes.
distractorRationale: A oppositeResult: If basil’s airborne chemicals repelled aphids, nearby tomatoes should have fewer aphids, not more; this result points against the hypothesis.
B unrelatedMeasuredVariable: Fruit production is not the outcome in the hypothesis, which concerns aphid infestations only.
D nearbyHypothesis: Shows that aphids avoid basil itself, a related claim, but says nothing about whether basil’s airborne chemicals protect neighboring tomato plants.

stimulus: Song sparrows living in cities often sing with higher minimum frequencies (the lowest pitch in a song) than rural song sparrows do. Because traffic noise is concentrated at low frequencies, ecologist Tomás Ferreira hypothesizes that this difference is not a fixed trait of urban populations. Instead, he proposes that individual urban sparrows adjust their songs moment to moment, raising the minimum frequency when traffic noise increases and lowering it again when the noise subsides. To test this idea, Ferreira recorded the songs of urban and rural sparrows under varying noise conditions.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Ferreira’s hypothesis?
choices: Urban sparrows sang fewer songs per hour during weekday rush hour than during light Sunday-morning traffic.
Urban sparrows sang at higher minimum frequencies, on average, than did rural sparrows recorded during the same weeks.
Urban sparrows sang at minimum frequencies just as high during light Sunday-morning traffic as during weekday rush hour.
Rural sparrows exposed to playback of recorded traffic noise raised the minimum frequencies of their songs within minutes.
explanation: Pin down what the hypothesis predicts: if pitch tracks noise moment to moment, urban birds should drop their minimum frequency when traffic is light. A finding that urban birds keep the same high pitch in quiet Sunday traffic contradicts that prediction and instead fits a fixed difference between populations. That is choice C. The most tempting wrong choice, B, merely restates the urban–rural gap, which both the flexible and the fixed explanations predict.

pipeline.governingClue: "individual urban sparrows adjust their songs moment to moment, raising the minimum frequency when traffic noise increases and lowering it again when the noise subsides"
distractorRationale: A unrelatedMeasuredVariable: Song rate is not song pitch; the hypothesis concerns only the minimum frequency of songs, so a change in how often sparrows sing neither supports nor weakens it.

B nonDiscriminating: Higher urban pitch is the starting observation and would be expected whether the difference is a moment-to-moment adjustment or a fixed population trait, so it cannot weaken the hypothesis.
D oppositeResult: Birds raising their pitch quickly in response to added noise is exactly what a flexible, moment-to-moment adjustment predicts, so this supports rather than weakens the hypothesis.

stimulus: In Aurelio Massey’s 1912 novel The Harbor Clerk, the narrator, Edwin Tolle, spends his days recording cargo shipments for a small trading firm. Throughout the novel, Tolle dismisses his job as dull and unimportant even as he reveals that he takes real pride in the care with which he performs it:
stem: Which quotation from The Harbor Clerk most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: “I rule every column with the same steel edge and check each sum twice, for a ledger, I have always held, should be as spotless as a chapel floor.”
“Copying cargo lists is drowsy work that any schoolboy could manage, yet I defy anyone to find a single blotted figure in my books from these eleven years.”
“Mr. Hale praises my ledgers to every captain who comes through the door, though in eleven years he has not once thought to raise my wages.”
“The hours at the desk crawl past, each one exactly like the last, until even the gulls on the pier seem more usefully employed than I am.”
explanation: Split the claim into two checks: (1) Tolle calls the job dull or unimportant, and (2) he shows pride in doing it carefully. Only B does both: “drowsy work that any schoolboy could manage” belittles the job, and his boast that no one could find a blotted figure shows pride in his precision. A and D each satisfy only one half. The most tempting wrong choice, A, shows careful work but never dismisses the job.

pipeline.governingClue: "drowsy work that any schoolboy could manage" (dismissal) + "I defy anyone to find a single blotted figure in my books" (pride in care)
distractorRationale: A partBOnly: Shows Tolle’s pride in careful work (ruled columns, sums checked twice) but never dismisses the job as dull or unimportant.

C other: Presents the employer’s praise and Tolle’s complaint about pay; neither Tolle’s own dismissal of the work nor his own pride in it is expressed, so it shifts the attitude to another character.
D partAOnly: Conveys that the work feels tedious and pointless but says nothing about the care Tolle takes or any pride in doing it well.

stimulus:
| Flower color | Bee visits at Site A (number) | Bee visits at Site B (number) |
|---|---|---|
| Purple | 48 | 52 |
| Yellow | 21 | 25 |
| White | 30 | 19 |

Ecologist Rafael Duarte counted how many times bees landed on flowers of three colors in two meadows, Site A and Site B, during one summer morning. Duarte claims that at Site B, bees visited purple flowers more often than they visited yellow flowers. ______
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Duarte’s claim?
choices: At Site B, bees made 52 visits to purple flowers and 19 visits to white flowers.
At Site A, bees made 48 visits to purple flowers and 21 visits to yellow flowers.
At Site B, bees made 52 visits to purple flowers and 25 visits to yellow flowers.
Bees made 48 visits to purple flowers at Site A and 52 visits at Site B.
explanation: Find the claim's three parts: Site B, purple flowers, yellow flowers. Then pick the choice that uses all three. In the Site B column, purple (52) is greater than yellow (25), so C supports the claim. A is tempting because it uses Site B and purple, but it compares purple with white, not yellow.

pipeline.governingClue: Site B column: Purple 52 vs. Yellow 25.
distractorRationale: A wrongComparisonPair: The numbers are accurate for Site B, but the choice compares purple with white flowers, not purple with yellow flowers as the claim requires.
B irrelevantSeries: The choice compares the right flower colors, but it uses Site A data, and the claim is only about Site B.
D singleSeries: The choice reports only purple-flower visits (at both sites) and gives no yellow-flower data, so it cannot show the comparison in the claim.

stimulus:
| Good | Amount shipped in 1880 (tons) | Amount shipped in 1900 (tons) |
|---|---|---|
| Coal | 1,200 | 6,400 |
| Timber | 6,800 | 7,000 |
| Grain | 4,500 | 2,100 |

Historian Ilse Varga studied shipping records from Port Halden, a small river town, to learn how its trade changed between 1880 and 1900. She found that the amount of coal moving through the port rose sharply over that period: ______
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: grain shipments fell from 4,500 tons in 1880 to 2,100 tons in 1900.
coal shipments grew from 1,200 tons in 1880 to 6,400 tons in 1900.
timber shipments reached 7,000 tons in 1900, the most of any good.
coal shipments totaled 1,200 tons in 1880, the least of any good.
explanation: The statement is about coal and a rise over time, so you need coal's amount in both years. The coal row goes from 1,200 tons to 6,400 tons, which is a sharp increase. Only B gives both numbers. C is tempting because 7,000 is the largest number in the table, but it is about timber's final total, not coal's change.

distractorRationale: A irrelevantSeries: The grain figures are accurate, but the statement is about coal, not grain.
C finalValueNotChange: It reports timber's highest 1900 total, but the statement is about how coal changed over time, and timber barely changed.
D other: It cites only coal's 1880 starting amount and leaves out the 1900 amount, so it cannot show that coal shipments rose.

stimulus: Caddisfly larvae protect their soft bodies by building portable cases from stones they gather on streambeds. Ecologist Ifeoma Adeyemi found that larvae living below hydroelectric dams, where water is periodically released in strong surges, use larger stones in their cases than larvae living upstream do. One explanation is that dams trap fine sediment, leaving mostly larger stones available downstream. Adeyemi, however, hypothesizes that the larvae actively select larger, heavier stones when they experience strong currents, since cases made of such stones are harder for water to sweep away. To test this, she collected larvae from below a dam, removed their cases, and placed the larvae in laboratory tanks containing equal amounts of small and large stones. Some tanks had fast-moving water, and others had slow-moving water.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Adeyemi’s hypothesis?
choices: Larvae in the fast-flow tanks built cases with a larger average stone size than did larvae in the slow-flow tanks.
Larvae in the fast-flow tanks built cases with about the same average stone size as did larvae in the slow-flow tanks.
Streambeds below the dam contained a higher proportion of large stones than did streambeds upstream of the dam.
Larvae in the fast-flow tanks took longer to finish building their cases than did larvae in the slow-flow tanks.
explanation: Identify what the hypothesis predicts in the experiment: with both stone sizes equally available, fast-flow larvae should choose larger stones than slow-flow larvae. A finding of no difference between the fast- and slow-flow tanks shows that current does not drive stone choice, which directly weakens the hypothesis. That result also points instead to stone availability as the explanation. Most tempting wrong choice: C restates the rival's premise about sediment, but it is consistent with Adeyemi's hypothesis too, so it weakens nothing.

pipeline.governingClue: "the larvae actively select larger, heavier stones when they experience strong currents" combined with the test design: equal amounts of small and large stones, fast vs. slow water.
distractorRationale: A oppositeResult: Choosing larger stones under fast flow when both sizes are equally available is exactly what Adeyemi's hypothesis predicts, so this supports rather than weakens it.

C nonDiscriminating: Adeyemi does not deny that dams trap fine sediment; more large stones downstream is expected whether or not larvae actively select stones in response to current, so this does not undercut her hypothesis.
D unrelatedMeasuredVariable: Building time is not the variable the hypothesis concerns; the hypothesis is about which stone size larvae choose, and slower building says nothing about that choice.

stimulus:
Wildlife biologist Halima Yusuf filled backyard feeders with three different kinds of seed and counted how often birds visited each feeder in winter and in spring. She found that the birds' choices changed with the season and that at least one seed type became more popular from January to April. For example, ______

| Seed type | Visits per hour, January | Visits per hour, April |
|---|---|---|
| Sunflower | 42 | 31 |
| Millet | 18 | 24 |
| Thistle | 27 | 12 |
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
choices: sunflower seed feeders drew 31 visits per hour in April, the most of any seed type.
millet feeders drew 18 visits per hour in January and 24 visits per hour in April.
thistle feeders drew 27 visits per hour in January and 12 visits per hour in April.
millet feeders drew 18 visits per hour in January, while sunflower feeders drew 42.
explanation: The example must show one seed type getting more visits in April than in January. Scan each row left to right: sunflower and thistle both drop, and only millet rises (18 to 24). Choice B reports exactly that rise. The most tempting wrong answer, A, gives the biggest April number, but sunflower actually lost visits, so it shows a final value, not an increase.

pipeline.governingClue: Millet row: 18 visits per hour (January) → 24 visits per hour (April), the only increase in the table.
distractorRationale: A finalValueNotChange: Accurately reports the highest April value, but the claim is about a seed type becoming more popular; sunflower visits actually dropped from 42 to 31.
C wrongDirection: Accurately describes thistle across the two months, but visits fell from 27 to 12, the opposite of becoming more popular.
D wrongComparisonPair: Accurately compares millet with sunflower within January, but the claim requires comparing one seed type across January and April.

stimulus:
Historian Owen Castellanos studied newspaper sales in the port city of Halden around the turn of the twentieth century. In 1890, the Morning Ledger was the city's best-selling paper, selling more daily copies than its rival, the Evening Star. By 1910, however, ______

| Newspaper | Daily copies sold, 1890 | Daily copies sold, 1910 | Pages devoted to advertising, 1910 (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Morning Ledger | 12,400 | 15,100 | 38 |
| Evening Star | 8,700 | 21,300 | 45 |
| Harbor Gazette | 3,200 | 2,900 | 22 |
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: the Evening Star's daily sales had risen to 21,300 copies from 8,700 in 1890.
45 percent of the Evening Star's pages were advertising, compared with the Ledger's 38 percent.
the Evening Star was selling 21,300 daily copies, compared with the Ledger's 15,100.
the Harbor Gazette's daily sales had fallen to 2,900 copies from 3,200 in 1890.
explanation: The signal word "however" means the blank must reverse the 1890 situation: by 1910 the Evening Star must outsell the Ledger. Look only at the 1910 daily copies column: 21,300 for the Star beats 15,100 for the Ledger. Choice C states that comparison directly. The most tempting wrong answer, A, is true, but it describes only the Star's growth and never shows it passing the Ledger.

pipeline.governingClue: 1910 column: Evening Star 21,300 vs. Morning Ledger 15,100 daily copies.
distractorRationale: A singleSeries: Accurately describes the Evening Star's growth alone, but the statement needs a comparison showing the Star outselling the Ledger in 1910.
B countVsPercent: Uses the advertising-page percentages instead of the counts of daily copies sold, so it says nothing about which paper sold more.
D irrelevantSeries: Accurately reports the Harbor Gazette's sales, but the statement is only about the Ledger and the Star.
notes: Minor wording inconsistency: the passage says the historian studied sales 'in the early 1900s,' but the data include 1890, which is in the late 1800s. A phrase such as 'around the turn of the twentieth century' would be accurate. This does not affect the answer.
Reviewer edit: "in the early 1900s…" → "around the turn of the twentieth century…"

stimulus: Ecologist Rina Takeda noticed that hummingbirds in a mountain meadow had stopped visiting a patch of red columbine flowers. She first checked whether the flowers had stopped producing nectar, but their nectar levels were normal. She then counted the hummingbirds in the meadow and found that their numbers had not dropped. Takeda therefore concluded that the birds' avoidance of the patch ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: is happening in most mountain meadows where columbine grows.
has caused the columbine flowers to make more nectar than usual.
is probably caused by something other than nectar or bird numbers.
must be caused by a predator that hides near the patch.
explanation: This is a rule-out puzzle: Takeda tests two explanations and both fail. The only conclusion the evidence forces is that the cause must be something else. Choose the answer that simply follows from eliminating those two options. D is tempting because it names a specific cause, but nothing in the text points to a predator.

pipeline.governingClue: "nectar levels were normal" and "their numbers had not dropped" — both explanations are ruled out.
distractorRationale: A overgeneralization: Takeda studied one patch in one meadow; nothing supports a claim about most meadows.
B recycledWordsNewClaim: Reuses 'nectar' and 'columbine' but makes a new claim; the text says nectar levels were normal, not higher than usual.
D needsUnstatedPremise: The text never mentions predators; this conclusion requires an assumption the passage does not support.

stimulus: For many years, historians believed that only men worked as weavers in the town of Brenmoor during the 1600s, because the town's official weavers' guild listed only male members. Recently, however, researchers found the account books of several Brenmoor households. These books record payments made directly to women for weaving cloth. This discovery suggests that the guild's membership list ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: left out the women weavers of most towns in the region.
did not include everyone who wove cloth in Brenmoor.
shows exactly how many women wove cloth in Brenmoor.
was changed on purpose to hide the work of women.
explanation: The old belief rested on a guild list showing only men. The new records prove women were also paid to weave in Brenmoor. So the most modest conclusion is that the list missed some weavers. D is tempting, but the text gives no evidence that anyone left women off on purpose.

pipeline.governingClue: "These books record payments made directly to women for weaving cloth."
distractorRationale: A overgeneralization: The evidence concerns only Brenmoor; it says nothing about guild lists in most towns of the region.
C knownUnknownReversed: The guild list names no women, and the number of women weavers is still unknown; this treats an unknown as known.
D needsUnstatedPremise: Nothing in the text shows anyone's intent; claiming deliberate hiding requires an unsupported assumption.
notes: Distractor rationale wrong

Choice C is barely plausible. The passage says the guild list names only men, so a list that 'shows exactly how many women wove cloth' is flatly contradicted; few students would pick it. Its stated rationale (treating an unknown as known) also misdescribes the error, which is really a direct contradiction of the stimulus. Revise C into a real known/unknown reversal, e.g., a claim that the account books reveal how many women wove or that women outnumbered men.

stimulus: Marine biologist Tomás Ferreira studies two tide pools on the same rocky shore. Last spring, sea stars in both pools developed a wasting disease. The sea stars in the northern pool recovered within a few weeks, but those in the southern pool did not. Ferreira found that the water temperatures in the two pools were nearly identical. The pools also contained similar numbers of the mussels that the sea stars eat. These findings suggest that ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: sea stars on most rocky shores recover from wasting disease within a few weeks.
the faster recovery in the northern pool was caused by something other than temperature or food.
the sea stars in the southern pool ate fewer mussels than the northern sea stars did.
the northern sea stars had caught the disease before and had become resistant to it.
explanation: The pools differ in recovery, but Ferreira ruled out two possible causes: temperature (nearly identical) and food (similar numbers of mussels). The only conclusion the text forces is that some other factor explains the difference. Choice B says exactly that without naming a new cause. D is tempting, but nothing in the text mentions earlier infections or resistance.

pipeline.governingClue: "water temperatures in the two pools were nearly identical" and "similar numbers of the mussels": the two obvious explanations are both ruled out.
distractorRationale: A overgeneralization: The text describes only two pools on one shore, so it cannot support a claim about sea stars on most rocky shores.

C recycledWordsNewClaim: Reuses 'mussels' and 'eat' to make a claim about how much the sea stars ate, but the text says only that the pools held similar numbers of mussels, which points away from a food difference.
D needsUnstatedPremise: Requires an assumption about earlier infections and resistance that the text never mentions.

stimulus: A handwritten score of the song "Evening Lanterns" by composer Ilse Marten has long been dated to 1845, when Marten was a teenager. Recently, a librarian examined the paper the score is written on. She found a watermark showing that the paper came from the Hollen paper mill. Records show that the Hollen mill did not begin making paper until 1851. Therefore, the score itself ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: proves that Marten first composed the song in the year 1851.
suggests that all of Marten's early scores were dated incorrectly.
was most likely written down no earlier than the year 1851.
was printed at the Hollen mill during the year 1845.
explanation: Chain the facts: the score is on Hollen paper, and Hollen paper did not exist before 1851. So this written copy cannot be older than 1851, which is choice C. Notice the blank is about "the score itself," not the song. A is the tempting trap: the paper dates the copy, but the year Marten first composed the song remains unknown.

pipeline.governingClue: "the Hollen mill did not begin making paper until 1851": the paper, and so the writing on it, cannot be older than 1851.
distractorRationale: A knownUnknownReversed: The paper shows only when this copy could have been written. When Marten first composed the song is still unknown, and the score may be a later copy of an older song.
B overgeneralization: Extends a finding about one score to all of Marten's early scores.
D recycledWordsNewClaim: Reuses 'Hollen mill' and '1845' to claim the mill printed the score in 1845, but the mill made paper, and it did not start until 1851.
notes: Distractor rationale wrong

Choice D is implausible. It contradicts two explicit facts in the passage: the score is described as handwritten, not printed, and the mill did not begin making paper until 1851, so it could not have produced anything in 1845. Almost no student who has read the passage would pick it. It needs a more tempting recycled-words claim, for example one that misreads what the 1851 date tells us about the paper rather than one that negates the stated facts outright.

stimulus:
Ecologist Ruth Adeyemi grew sunflowers on farm plots edged with a strip of wildflowers, a strip of mowed grass, or no strip at all. She then counted bee visits to the sunflowers during two summers. Adeyemi claims that the advantage of wildflower strips over bare plot edges grew in the second summer, possibly because more bees had begun nesting in the strips. ______

| Plot edge | 2022 (visits per hour) | 2023 (visits per hour) |
|---|---|---|
| Wildflower strip | 14 | 21 |
| Mowed grass strip | 12 | 13 |
| No strip | 12 | 11 |
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Adeyemi’s claim?
choices: Plots with wildflower strips went from 14 to 21 visits per hour between 2022 and 2023.
Plots with mowed grass strips went from 12 to 13 visits per hour, while plots without strips went from 12 to 11.
Plots with mowed grass strips averaged 12 visits per hour in 2022 and 13 visits per hour in 2023.
Plots with wildflower strips went from 14 to 21 visits per hour, while plots without strips went from 12 to 11.
explanation: The claim compares two groups over time: wildflower-strip plots versus plots with no strip, in 2022 and 2023. Find the choice that cites both of those rows for both years. Wildflower plots rose from 14 to 21 while bare-edge plots dipped from 12 to 11, so the advantage widened. A is the tempting trap: it shows wildflower plots improving but gives no bare-edge baseline, so it cannot show a growing advantage.

pipeline.governingClue: Wildflower strip: 14 → 21; No strip: 12 → 11 (the gap widens from 2022 to 2023).
distractorRationale: A singleSeries: Accurately reports the rise for wildflower plots, but the claim concerns the advantage of wildflower strips over bare edges, which requires comparison with the no-strip plots.
B wrongComparisonPair: Accurately compares mowed-grass plots with no-strip plots, but the claim compares wildflower strips with bare edges.
C irrelevantSeries: Accurately describes the mowed-grass plots, a series the claim is not about.

stimulus:
In 2012, marine ecologist Rafael Mendes and colleagues began replanting seagrass in Halden Bay, one of three neighboring bays on the same stretch of coast; Corrie Bay and Ostra Bay were left unplanted. Because water quality improved along the whole coastline during the following decade, a rise in Halden Bay's seagrass cover would not by itself show that the replanting worked. Even so, the team's measurements suggest that the replanting made a difference: from 2012 to 2022, ______

| Bay | Seagrass cover, 2012 (% of sea floor) | Seagrass cover, 2022 (% of sea floor) |
|---|---|---|
| Corrie Bay | 41 | 46 |
| Halden Bay | 12 | 35 |
| Ostra Bay | 28 | 30 |
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: Corrie Bay kept the greatest seagrass cover of the three bays, ending the decade at 46% of the sea floor.
seagrass cover in Halden Bay nearly tripled, climbing from 12% of the sea floor to 35% of the sea floor.
cover rose from 12% to 35% in Halden Bay but changed by only a few percentage points in the other two bays.
seagrass cover rose more in Corrie Bay, from 41% to 46%, than it did in Ostra Bay, from 28% to 30%.
explanation: The passage rules out evidence about Halden Bay alone because water quality improved everywhere. To show replanting mattered, you need the replanted bay's gain to stand out against the unplanted bays' gains: Halden rose 23 points, while Corrie and Ostra rose only 5 and 2. Only C makes that comparison. B is the most tempting, but it reports Halden's rise alone, which is exactly what the passage says is not enough.

pipeline.governingClue: "a rise in Halden Bay's seagrass cover would not by itself show that the replanting worked" — so the completion must contrast Halden's change (12→35) with the small changes in the unplanted bays (41→46, 28→30).
distractorRationale: A finalValueNotChange: Accurately reports Corrie Bay's highest 2022 value, but the statement is about how much each bay changed, and Corrie Bay was not replanted.
B singleSeries: Accurate about Halden Bay alone, but the passage says a Halden rise by itself cannot rule out coastwide improvement; the replanted bay must be compared with the unplanted bays.
D wrongComparisonPair: Accurate, but compares the two unplanted bays with each other, which says nothing about whether replanting helped Halden Bay.

stimulus:
Great tits in noisy cities often sing with a higher minimum frequency than forest birds, possibly so that low-pitched traffic rumble does not mask their songs. To test whether a population shifts its songs as noise rises and falls, ornithologist Hana Lindqvist recorded songs on weekday and Sunday mornings at a city-center site and at a forest site. She claims that the city birds' weekday change reflects traffic noise rather than any weekly rhythm in the birds' own behavior, noting that ______

| Site | Traffic noise, weekday mornings (decibels) | Traffic noise, Sunday mornings (decibels) | Minimum song frequency, weekday mornings (kHz) | Minimum song frequency, Sunday mornings (kHz) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| City center | 71 | 54 | 3.6 | 3.1 |
| Forest | 38 | 37 | 2.9 | 2.9 |
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Lindqvist’s claim?
choices: on weekday mornings, the city birds' minimum song frequency (3.6 kHz) was well above that of the forest birds (2.9 kHz).
the city birds' minimum frequency was 3.6 kHz on weekdays and 3.1 kHz on Sundays, while the forest birds' was 2.9 kHz on both.
the city birds' minimum song frequency was 3.6 kHz on weekday mornings but only 3.1 kHz on Sunday mornings.
traffic noise at the city site averaged 71 decibels on weekday mornings but only 54 decibels on Sunday mornings.
explanation: Lindqvist must rule out a weekday effect that would occur anywhere. The forest site is the control: its noise barely changes, and its birds' minimum frequency stays at 2.9 kHz on both days. Meanwhile, the city birds shift from 3.6 to 3.1 kHz as noise drops, so the change follows noise rather than the day of the week. Only B pairs the city change with the unchanged forest value. C is the most tempting, but it shows the city change alone, which cannot rule out a weekly rhythm shared by all birds.

pipeline.governingClue: "rather than any weekly rhythm in the birds' own behavior" — ruling out a weekly rhythm requires the forest control: city 3.6 vs. 3.1 kHz, but forest 2.9 kHz on both days, where noise barely changed (38 vs. 37 dB).
distractorRationale: A wrongComparisonPair: Accurate, but compares the two sites on the same day instead of comparing weekdays with Sundays; a fixed difference between populations would produce the same result.
C singleSeries: Accurate about the city birds only; without the forest birds' unchanged values, a weekly rhythm shared by all birds could explain the weekday rise.
D irrelevantSeries: Accurate, but reports the traffic-noise columns rather than song frequency, so it shows that noise varies without showing any change in the birds' songs.

stimulus:
Plant physiologist Rahel Tesfaye compared a widely grown sorghum variety, S-12, with DT-3, a variety bred for dry regions, and with a wild relative of sorghum. After the plants were fully watered, irrigation was stopped, and Tesfaye tracked the water content of their leaves for two weeks. DT-3 is often assumed to withstand drought because its leaves store more water from the outset. Tesfaye claims instead that DT-3's advantage over S-12 comes from losing water more slowly once irrigation ends, noting that ______

| Plant | Leaf water content, day 0 (%) | Leaf water content, day 7 (%) | Leaf water content, day 14 (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| S-12 | 86 | 74 | 61 |
| DT-3 | 70 | 66 | 58 |
| Wild relative | 74 | 69 | 63 |
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Tesfaye’s claim?
choices: on day 14, the leaves of S-12 still held more water (61%) than did the leaves of DT-3 (58%).
the leaf water content of the wild relative fell from 74% to 63% over 14 days, whereas that of S-12 fell from 86% to 61%.
the leaf water content of DT-3 fell from 70% to 58% over 14 days, whereas that of S-12 fell from 86% to 61%.
the leaves of S-12 held more water than did the leaves of DT-3 on day 0 (86% versus 70%), as did those of the wild relative (74%).
explanation: Break the claim into its two parts: DT-3 does not start with more leaf water than S-12, and DT-3 loses water more slowly. Only C gives both varieties' starting and ending values, showing DT-3 began lower (70% vs. 86%) yet dropped far less (12 points vs. 25). A and D each report a single day, so neither shows a rate of loss. B is the most tempting wrong choice: it has the right shape, but it is about the wild relative, not DT-3.

pipeline.governingClue: Claim has two parts: DT-3 does not start with more water, and it loses water more slowly than S-12. DT-3: 70% → 58% (drop of 12); S-12: 86% → 61% (drop of 25).
distractorRationale: A finalValueNotChange: Accurately reports day 14 values only; a single end point says nothing about how quickly each variety lost water, which is what the claim is about.
B wrongComparisonPair: Accurately shows a smaller decline for a low-starting plant, but that plant is the wild relative, not DT-3; the claim compares DT-3 with S-12.
D other: Half-right: the day 0 values rebut the 'stores more water from the outset' assumption, but no choice data show the rate of water loss, the actual substance of Tesfaye's claim.
notes: Off-pattern
Distractor rationale wrong

Internal tension: the table shows S-12 has higher leaf water content than DT-3 on every day, including day 14 (61% vs 58%), so the data never show the 'advantage over S-12' the claim presupposes. Choice A even highlights this. Adjusting the values so DT-3 ends above S-12 on day 14 (e.g., S-12 at 55%) would make the scenario coherent while keeping C as the key.

The stimulus contradicts itself. Tesfaye's claim assumes DT-3 has an advantage over S-12, but the table never shows DT-3 ahead: S-12 holds more leaf water on every day, including day 14 (61% vs. 58%). A careful student can reasonably doubt that the data support any DT-3 advantage. Revise the values, for example so DT-3 ends higher than S-12 despite starting lower, or reword the claim.

Because of that conflict, choice A directly undercuts the premise of the claim rather than being merely irrelevant. This makes the item's logic murky, and the stated reason for A (that a single end point says nothing about rate) understates how A interacts with the claim.

The stated reason for D says 'no choice data show the rate of water loss.' Read literally, this says no answer choice shows the rate, which is false because C does. It should say that D's data show only starting values, not the rate of loss.

The key requires students to compute two declines (12 vs. 25 points) rather than simply read and compare values. This is minor, since the 'fell from X to Y' format is common, but it edges past the pattern's no-calculation constraint.

stimulus:
Musicologist Ilse Vandermeer argues that critics who simply count the works by living composers that orchestras perform overlook a subtler shift. Because many orchestras have trimmed their seasons in recent decades, works by living composers can make up a larger portion of an orchestra's season even when fewer of them are performed. For example, ______

| Orchestra | Works by living composers, 1995 (number) | Works by living composers, 1995 (% of season) | Works by living composers, 2020 (number) | Works by living composers, 2020 (% of season) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 22 | 15 | 30 | 21 |
| B | 18 | 12 | 15 | 15 |
| C | 16 | 10 | 12 | 8 |
| D | 20 | 14 | 21 | 12 |
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
choices: Orchestra A performed 22 works by living composers in 1995 (15% of its season) and 30 such works in 2020 (21% of its season).
Orchestra B performed 18 works by living composers in 1995 (12% of its season) and 15 such works in 2020 (15% of its season).
Orchestra C performed 16 works by living composers in 1995 (10% of its season) and 12 such works in 2020 (8% of its season).
Orchestra D performed 20 works by living composers in 1995 (14% of its season) and 21 such works in 2020 (12% of its season).
explanation: The example needs two things at once: the number of works by living composers falls, and their share of the season rises. Check each row for count down and percent up; only Orchestra B fits (18 → 15 works, 12% → 15% of the season). A and C each match only one half, since their count and percent move together. D is the most tempting wrong choice because its count and percent move in opposite directions, but in the reverse order: count up, share down.

pipeline.governingClue: Orchestra B row: number fell from 18 to 15 while % of season rose from 12 to 15.
distractorRationale: A other: Half-right: the share rose (15% to 21%), but the number of works also rose (22 to 30), so it lacks the 'fewer works performed' half of the example.
C other: Half-right: the number of works fell (16 to 12), but the share also fell (10% to 8%), so it lacks the 'larger portion' half of the example.
D wrongDirection: Accurate data showing the reverse pattern: the number of works rose slightly (20 to 21) while the share of the season fell (14% to 12%).

stimulus: Biologist Amara Okafor observed that tree frogs on a small island call at a higher pitch than frogs of the same species on the nearby mainland. Smaller frogs often produce higher-pitched calls, but Okafor found no difference in body size between the island and mainland frogs. Dense vegetation can also favor higher pitches, which pass more clearly through leaves, yet the mainland sites Okafor studied were just as densely vegetated as the island. One difference remained: the island frogs share their habitat with a loud insect whose buzzing overlaps the lower frequencies of the frogs' calls, and no such insect lives at the mainland sites. Okafor's findings therefore suggest that ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: frogs in most island habitats raise the pitch of their calls so that they are not drowned out by insects.
the insect's presence, not frog size or vegetation, may account for the island frogs' higher-pitched calls.
the island frogs developed higher-pitched calls by imitating the insect's buzzing over many generations.
the insect's buzzing travels more clearly through the island's dense vegetation than the frogs' calls do.
explanation: Track the eliminations: size is ruled out, vegetation is ruled out, and the only remaining difference is the insect whose noise overlaps the frogs' lower frequencies. The modest conclusion is that the insect may explain the pitch difference, which is exactly what B says, hedged with 'may.' Choices that go beyond this one comparison or add a mechanism the text never mentions overreach. A is the most tempting wrong choice, but it stretches one island study into a rule about most island frogs.

pipeline.governingClue: Body size and vegetation are each ruled out ('no difference in body size'; 'just as densely vegetated'), leaving only the insect: 'One difference remained.'
distractorRationale: A overgeneralization: Okafor studied one island and one mainland area; nothing supports a claim about frogs in most island habitats.

C needsUnstatedPremise: Requires an unsupported assumption that frogs learn calls by imitation; the passage gives no evidence of imitation, and the insect's buzz overlaps the lower frequencies, so copying it would not explain a higher pitch.
D recycledWordsNewClaim: Reuses 'buzzing,' 'travels more clearly,' and 'dense vegetation' to make a new comparison of sound transmission that the passage never addresses.

stimulus: For decades, historians assumed that the glass beads excavated at a fifteenth-century market town along the Niger River had been made in Venice, because the beads' chemical makeup closely matches that of Venetian glass from the period. Archaeologist Kwame Asante has now shown that some Egyptian glass workshops of the same century used an identical plant-ash recipe, producing glass that is chemically indistinguishable from Venetian glass. Asante also notes that the town's merchants traded regularly with partners in both Egypt and southern Europe. Taken together, these findings imply that ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the beads were more likely produced in Egypt than in Venice, given the town's trading ties to Egypt.
most glass objects that historians have attributed to Venetian workshops were in fact made elsewhere.
Egyptian and Venetian glassmakers probably exchanged their plant-ash recipe through the town's merchants.
the beads' chemical makeup cannot by itself establish whether they were made in Venice or in Egypt.
explanation: The old conclusion rested on a single premise: the chemistry matches Venice. Asante shows the same chemistry also matches Egypt, and the trade evidence points to both places equally. So the chemical evidence alone no longer decides the question. That is the most modest conclusion the premises force, and it is D. A is the most tempting wrong choice, but it swaps one unproven origin for another even though the trade evidence favors neither place.

pipeline.governingClue: "producing glass that is chemically indistinguishable from Venetian glass" combined with trade ties to "both Egypt and southern Europe."
distractorRationale: A needsUnstatedPremise: The town traded with both Egypt and southern Europe, so favoring Egypt requires an unstated assumption that Egyptian trade was more important or more likely to supply beads.
B overgeneralization: Extends a finding about one set of beads to most objects ever attributed to Venice, and turns 'possibly elsewhere' into 'in fact elsewhere.'
C recycledWordsNewClaim: Reuses 'plant-ash recipe' and 'merchants' to invent a claim about how the recipe spread, which the passage never discusses.

stimulus: Botanists have long assumed that the stems of a certain morning glory species wrap around supports because the growing tip bends toward light, which often strikes a pole or branch from one side. To test this idea, plant biologist Amara Okonjo grew seedlings beside wooden stakes in two chambers: one lit from the side and one kept completely dark. After three weeks, the seedlings in both chambers had wrapped around their stakes the same number of times and in the same direction. These results suggest that ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: most climbing plants wrap around their supports without responding to light at all.
the seedlings find their stakes by sensing physical contact with them instead.
light is not required for seedlings of this species to wrap around a support.
light has no influence on any part of how this morning glory species grows.
explanation: The old assumption is that light causes the wrapping. Seedlings in total darkness wrapped exactly as much as lit ones, so light cannot be necessary for wrapping in this species. That is all the evidence forces. The tempting D goes too far: only wrapping was measured, not every part of the plant's growth.

pipeline.governingClue: "the seedlings in both chambers had wrapped around their stakes the same number of times and in the same direction"
distractorRationale: A overgeneralization: The experiment tested one morning glory species, so it cannot support a claim about most climbing plants.
B needsUnstatedPremise: The text never says how the seedlings detect their stakes; choosing touch as the mechanism requires an assumption the experiment did not test.
D other: Stretches a result about wrapping alone to every aspect of growth (height, leaves, flowering), none of which was measured, so it overstates the finding's scope.

stimulus: In 2022, the Elm Street branch of a city's public library recorded 40 percent more weekday morning visitors than it had in 2021. Library staff considered several explanations. The branch's opening hours were identical in both years, and it added no new morning programs. Nor had any nearby branch closed, which might have sent its patrons to Elm Street. One change did occur in 2022, however: the city moved a bus stop from three blocks away to the sidewalk directly outside the Elm Street branch. Taken together, these facts suggest that ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: most of the branch's additional weekday morning visitors in 2022 traveled there by bus.
moving the bus stop may have contributed to the branch's rise in weekday morning visitors.
relocating bus stops near libraries raises visitor numbers at most library branches.
staff were unable to confirm whether the branch's opening hours had changed from 2021 to 2022.
explanation: The passage rules out explanations one by one: same hours, no new programs, no nearby closure. The one remaining change is the bus stop, so the modest conclusion is that it may have contributed to the increase. Note the hedge "may have"; the evidence does not prove more. The tempting A sounds like the same idea but adds a claim about how most visitors traveled, which the text never measures.

pipeline.governingClue: "One change did occur in 2022, however: the city moved a bus stop... directly outside the Elm Street branch."
distractorRationale: A needsUnstatedPremise: The text gives no data on how visitors arrived; claiming most came by bus assumes a travel pattern the staff never recorded.
C overgeneralization: Extends the experience of a single branch to most library branches.
D knownUnknownReversed: The text states the opening hours were identical in both years, so this choice treats a known fact as unknown.

stimulus: The museum's new exhibit on ancient Egyptian glassmaking is deliberately ______: visitors can handle replica tools, pump air into a model furnace, and try shaping warm wax "glass" with their own hands.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The colon signals that what follows explains the blank. Every example describes visitors actively taking part, so the exhibit is "interactive." Choose the word that the examples actually illustrate, not a word linked to the topic. The most tempting wrong choice, C, is about glass breaking, not about visitors participating.

pipeline.governingClue: visitors can handle replica tools, pump air into a model furnace, and try shaping warm wax "glass" with their own hands
distractorRationale: A antonymTone: "Passive" means involving no active participation, the opposite of an exhibit where visitors handle tools, pump air, and shape materials themselves.
C topicAssociated: "Fragile" fits the topic of glass, but the clue after the colon describes visitor participation, not how easily something breaks.
D topicAssociated: "Translucent" describes glass itself, but the clue is about what visitors get to do, not about how light passes through the objects.

stimulus: Marcus was usually ______ during class discussions, rarely raising his hand or sharing his opinions. During the school debate, however, he surprised everyone by speaking confidently for ten minutes.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The phrase right after the blank defines it: Marcus rarely raises his hand or shares his opinions. "However" then contrasts this with his confident speaking. A person who holds back from speaking is "reserved." The most tempting wrong choice, B, uses a different sense of "reserved" (held in advance), not the personality sense.

pipeline.governingClue: rarely raising his hand or sharing his opinions
distractorRationale: A antonymTone: "Talkative" is the opposite of someone who rarely raises his hand or shares opinions, and it would make the debate performance unsurprising.
B commonDictionarySense: "Booked" matches "reserved" only in the sense of a seat or table held in advance, not the sense of a quiet, restrained person.
D topicAssociated: "Academic" relates to school and class discussions, but it does not describe someone who rarely speaks up.
notes: Distractor rationale wrong

Choice B ("booked") is not plausible. It is a synonym of a different sense of the key word (a reservation), so it can only tempt a student who has already thought of "reserved." A student who doesn't know the key has no reason to pick it, since "booked" has no meaning that fits a quiet student. The stated rationale explains how the item writer built the choice, not an error a student would actually make. Replace it with a word whose common meaning seems to fit the context, or with a near-miss in tone or degree (e.g., "distracted" or "indifferent").

stimulus: Plant ecologist Ines Varga collected seeds of a desert wildflower from two populations, one on a rocky plateau and one in a sandy basin. When sown in identical greenhouse soil and watered on the same schedule, the plateau seeds germinated at less than half the rate of the basin seeds. Inspection showed no insect damage to either set, and all seeds had been gathered in the same week at the same stage of ripeness. When Varga lightly scratched the seed coats, the plateau seeds germinated at nearly the same rate as the basin seeds, whereas scratching made no difference to the basin seeds' germination rate. Varga therefore concluded that the plateau seeds' lower germination rate most likely results from ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: seed coats that restrict germination in most wildflower species native to desert regions.
damage to the plateau seeds' coats that occurred while the seeds were still ripening.
a property of the plateau seeds' coats that is not shared by the basin seeds' coats.
the plateau's rocky terrain, which favored plants that produce especially tough seed coats.
explanation: List what the text eliminates. Soil, watering, insect damage, and ripeness are all ruled out. Scratching the coats removed the gap, and it helped only the plateau seeds, so something about the plateau seeds' coats, absent in the basin seeds, holds back germination. The text never explains why the coats differ, so the right answer stops at the coat difference itself. D is the most tempting wrong choice because it sounds plausible, but it adds a cause (rocky terrain favoring tough coats) that the text never mentions.

pipeline.governingClue: Scratching brought the plateau seeds up to nearly the basin rate but made no difference to the basin seeds.
distractorRationale: A overgeneralization: Extends a finding about one population to most desert species. The basin seeds, from the same species, were unaffected by scratching, so their coats do not restrict germination.
B other: Reverses the direction of the evidence. Scratching, a form of coat damage, raised germination, so coat damage would increase germination rather than lower it.
D needsUnstatedPremise: Offers an evolutionary cause tied to terrain. The text says nothing about why the coats differ, so this claim depends on an assumption the passage never supports.

stimulus: Since the 1920s, the landscape Harbor at Dusk has been attributed to the painter Edvard Lindqvist, who died in 1831. Recent analysis by conservator Mara Okafor detected a synthetic blue pigment that was not manufactured until 1842, leading some scholars to declare the attribution mistaken. Okafor found this pigment only in the upper sky, however. There it lies over a layer of an older natural blue, a pigment widely used by painters of Lindqvist's era. No trace of the synthetic blue appears anywhere beneath the painting's surface layers. These findings suggest that ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: Lindqvist painted the original sky himself before a later artist covered it with synthetic blue.
the presence of the synthetic blue does not, by itself, show that someone other than Lindqvist made the painting.
the painting was in fact made by Lindqvist, just as scholars in the 1920s had claimed.
many paintings from the early 1800s were altered by later restorers who used synthetic pigments.
explanation: Ask what the pigment evidence can and cannot prove. The 1842 pigment sits only on the surface, over an older layer, so it reflects a later alteration and cannot by itself disprove the attribution. The older layer is a common pigment of the era, so the evidence does not confirm Lindqvist either. The modest conclusion is that this objection fails, nothing more. A is the most tempting wrong choice: it assumes the underlying sky is Lindqvist's work, which the text never establishes.

pipeline.governingClue: The synthetic blue appears only in the surface of the upper sky, over an older pigment common in Lindqvist's era, and nowhere beneath the surface layers.
distractorRationale: A needsUnstatedPremise: Assumes the older blue layer is Lindqvist's own work. The text says only that this pigment was widely used in his era, so anyone of that period could have applied it.

C knownUnknownReversed: Treats an attribution that merely has not been disproved as one that has been confirmed. The evidence removes one objection but offers no positive proof that Lindqvist painted the work.
D overgeneralization: Extends evidence about one altered painting to many paintings of the period, which the single case cannot support.

stimulus: Peat moss, which grows in waterlogged bogs, can ______ remarkable amounts of water: a handful of dried moss placed in a bucket will soak up and hold as much as twenty times its own weight in liquid.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The colon signals that the second clause restates the blank. The moss "soak[s] up and hold[s]" water, so the blank must mean "keep" or "hold." "Retain" means exactly that. The most tempting wrong choice is A: "release" sounds scientific but means the opposite of holding.

pipeline.governingClue: "will soak up and hold as much as twenty times its own weight in liquid"
distractorRationale: A antonymTone: "Release" means to let go of. That is the opposite of the clue, which says the moss soaks up and holds water.
C topicAssociated: "Irrigate" relates to water and plants, but it means to supply water to land. The clue describes the moss holding water, not delivering it.
D commonDictionarySense: "Hire" matches a different sense of "retain," as in retaining a lawyer. That employment sense makes no sense for moss and water.
notes: Distractor rationale wrong

Distractor D ('hire') is implausible and eliminated instantly, which weakens the item's difficulty. Replacing it with a plausible near-synonym trap such as 'contain' or 'absorb' would make it a better test of precision.

Minor: 'peat moss' commonly refers to the dead, partially decomposed sphagnum harvested from bogs, though the living sphagnum is also called peat moss. The 'up to twenty times its weight' figure is consistent with commonly cited values (about 16–26x), so there is no factual error.
Choice D ("hire") is not plausible. No student reading about moss and water would pick it, so it is effectively a throwaway option and the item has only three functional choices.

The stated reason for D does not describe a student error. It explains how the writer built the distractor (a synonym of a different sense of the key, as in retaining a lawyer). No student error leads to choosing "hire" here. A real commonDictionarySense trap would use a word whose familiar meaning seems to fit the context on a quick reading.

stimulus: When critic Amara Diallo opened the debut collection by poet Tomás Reyes, she expected the poems to be ______, as many first books are; instead, she found them surprisingly polished, with nearly every line showing signs of careful revision.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: "Instead" signals a contrast between what Diallo expected and what she found. She found the poems "polished" and carefully revised, so she must have expected them to be rough or lacking polish. "Unrefined" captures that meaning. The most tempting wrong choice is A: "sophisticated" describes what she found, not the opposite she expected.

distractorRationale: A antonymTone: "Sophisticated" means refined and skillful, which is close to "polished." The word "instead" requires the opposite of what she actually found.
B topicAssociated: "Lyrical" fits the topic of poetry, but it does not contrast with "polished" or carefully revised.
C commonDictionarySense: "Unprocessed" matches the industrial sense of "unrefined" (unrefined sugar or oil). It does not describe the quality of writing.
notes: Distractor rationale wrong

Choice C ('unprocessed') is a near-synonym of the key and is arguably defensible. Raw, unrevised early poems could be described as 'unprocessed' in the sense of 'not worked over,' which directly contrasts with 'careful revision.' This weakens single-key clarity. The rationale's claim that it 'does not describe the quality of writing' is overstated. A sharper distractor (e.g., a word tied only to an unrelated sense) would avoid a possible double key.

stimulus: Because sediment cores from Ethiopia's Lake Tana record rainfall only indirectly, through shifts in pollen and mineral content, geochemist Ruth Abebe cautions that her reconstruction of the region's ancient monsoons is ______: the cores reveal whether a given century was wetter or drier than the one before it, but they cannot indicate how many millimeters of rain actually fell in any year.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The colon introduces a restatement of the missing word. The cores allow only comparisons (wetter or drier than the century before) and give no absolute measurements. A reconstruction built only on comparisons is relative. The most tempting wrong choice is C: approximate would mean rough rainfall totals, but the cores give no totals at all.

pipeline.governingClue: the cores reveal whether a given century was wetter or drier than the one before it, but they cannot indicate how many millimeters of rain actually fell
distractorRationale: A unlicensedConnotation: Provisional implies the reconstruction is temporary and awaiting revision. The text never suggests Abebe expects to change it. It describes only what kind of information the cores can give.

C other: This choice confuses having no measured amounts with having rough amounts. Approximate would mean the cores give estimated rainfall totals, but the text says they cannot indicate any amounts at all.
D antonymTone: Speculative suggests the reconstruction has little evidential basis. The clue says the opposite: the cores reliably show whether one century was wetter or drier than the last.

stimulus: In her letters from 1898, textile reformer Agnes Merrow hailed the new factory inspection law as a genuine victory for mill workers, yet she was careful to ______ that praise. In nearly every letter she reminded her correspondents that the law applied only to mills employing more than fifty people and that inspectors were required to visit each site just once a year.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The word 'yet' signals that Merrow's praise was held back in some way. The next sentence shows how: she kept pointing out the law's limits while still calling it a victory. To qualify a statement means to limit or restrict it, which is a secondary sense of a familiar word. The most tempting wrong choice is D: retract goes too far, because she never took back her praise.

pipeline.governingClue: hailed the new factory inspection law as a genuine victory... yet... reminded her correspondents that the law applied only to mills employing more than fifty people and that inspectors were required to visit each site just once a year
distractorRationale: A antonymTone: Justify means to support the praise with reasons. The details Merrow adds are limitations that weaken her praise, so they push in the opposite direction.
B topicAssociated: Publicize fits the idea of letter-writing and spreading news. However, the clue concerns how she limited her praise, not how widely she spread it.
D unlicensedConnotation: Retract implies Merrow withdrew her praise entirely. The text says she still called the law a genuine victory, so she only limited her praise.

stimulus: Historian Tomás Reyes argues that many sixteenth-century mapmakers regarded their charts of newly explored coastlines as ______. Rather than presenting these outlines as settled fact, the mapmakers often drew uncertain stretches of shore with faint dotted lines and left blank margins where later navigators could record corrections.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The second sentence restates the blank. The mapmakers did not treat the outlines as settled fact, and they expected later corrections. A word meaning "accepted for now but open to revision" fits, and that is "provisional." The most tempting wrong choice is "disposable": it also suggests something not final, but it implies the maps would be thrown out, while the text shows them being kept and improved.

pipeline.governingClue: "Rather than presenting these outlines as settled fact... left blank margins where later navigators could record corrections."
distractorRationale: A antonymTone: "Definitive" means final and authoritative, the opposite of charts deliberately left open to correction rather than presented "as settled fact."
B topicAssociated: "Nautical" fits the topic of navigators and coastlines but describes what the charts are about, not how the mapmakers regarded their accuracy.
D unlicensedConnotation: "Disposable" adds the idea that the charts were meant to be thrown away. The text says they were kept and corrected, so they were open to revision, not meant to be discarded.

stimulus: In the novel's opening chapter, bookseller Elias Varga is described as courteous but ______. He greets every customer with a polite nod and answers questions patiently, yet he never asks about their lives and rarely offers an opinion unless someone directly requests one.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The "but" signals that the blank qualifies "courteous," and the second sentence explains how. Elias is polite, yet he keeps to himself and holds back his opinions. A word meaning "restrained in sharing thoughts or feelings" fits, and that is "reserved." The most tempting wrong choice is "hostile": it also contrasts with warmth, but it adds an unfriendliness that contradicts his patience and politeness.

pipeline.governingClue: "he never asks about their lives and rarely offers an opinion unless someone directly requests one"
distractorRationale: A antonymTone: "Effusive" means openly and enthusiastically expressive, the opposite of someone who never asks about others and rarely shares opinions.
C topicAssociated: "Scholarly" suits a bookseller's setting, but the text describes how Elias holds back socially, not how learned he is.
D unlicensedConnotation: "Hostile" adds ill will that the text does not support. Elias is described as polite and patient; he is only quiet about personal matters.

stimulus: Many people picture the town libraries of the 1800s as quiet places used mainly by wealthy readers. However, records from several small libraries in the American Midwest tell a different story. Borrowing logs show that farmers, factory workers, and their children checked out books regularly, often walking miles to do so.
